question: What is JUnit and why does it exist? It provides a lightweight framework for writing and running repeatable unit tests in Java so that regressions are caught early and design feedback is continuous.
title: JUnit Testing
direct_answer: JUnit is the dominant unit-testing framework for Java, providing annotations (@Test, @BeforeEach, @ParameterizedTest), assertion methods (assertEquals, assertThrows, assertTrue), and a test runner that executes tests and reports failures. It exists because manual testing does not scale, and without automated tests, refactoring becomes a fear-driven activity where you avoid touching working code because you cannot verify it still works after changes. By making tests first-class code that runs in seconds, JUnit enables test-driven development, continuous integration, and the confidence to refactor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the purpose of unit testing, the JUnit lifecycle annotations, and the difference between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing tests that depend on order, share mutable state between tests, or test multiple concerns in a single test method.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain test-driven development (TDD), parameterized tests in JUnit 5, the AAA (Arrange-Act-Assert) pattern, and how mocking frameworks like Mockito isolate the unit under test.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: JUnit is a lightweight, open-source testing framework for Java that lets developers write self-checking, repeatable unit tests. A unit test exercises the smallest testable part of an application -- typically a single method or class -- in isolation from its dependencies. JUnit provides annotations to mark test methods (@Test) and lifecycle hooks (@BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAll), assertion methods to verify expected outcomes, and a test runner that discovers and executes tests, reporting pass or fail status. The current generation, JUnit 5 (Jupiter), introduced parameterized tests, dynamic tests, extension models, and lambda-based assertions. JUnit is the de facto standard for Java testing and is integrated into every major build tool (Maven, Gradle) and IDE (IntelliJ, Eclipse).

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: A unit test verifies the behavior of a single unit (method or class) in isolation, typically using stubs or mocks for external dependencies. The AAA pattern structures each test into three phases: Arrange (set up preconditions), Act (call the method under test), and Assert (verify the outcome). Lifecycle annotations control test fixture setup: @BeforeEach runs before each test method, @BeforeAll runs once per class, and @AfterEach/@AfterAll handle cleanup. JUnit 5 assertions are lambda-friendly: assertThrows checks that a specific exception is thrown, and assertAll groups multiple assertions so all are evaluated even if one fails. Parameterized tests (@ParameterizedTest) run the same test logic with different inputs, reducing duplication. The extension model (@ExtendWith) replaces JUnit 4's runner model, enabling custom dependency injection, mocking (MockitoExtension), and Spring context loading (SpringExtension).

sections.title: JUnit 4 vs JUnit 5 (Jupiter) Feature Comparison
rows: Generate tests at runtime from data

sections.title: JUnit 5 Test with Lifecycle, Assertions, and Parameterized Tests
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: Unit tests are fast (milliseconds) and isolate failures precisely, but they only test the unit in isolation, not the integration between components. Over-mocking can make tests brittle and tightly coupled to implementation details, causing tests to break on refactoring even when behavior is correct. Parameterized tests reduce duplication but make failure messages harder to interpret because the input is not visible in the test name. In practice, a healthy test pyramid has many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a small number of slow end-to-end tests at the top.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: JUnit is the standard Java unit-testing framework with annotations for test methods and lifecycle hooks.
The AAA pattern structures tests into Arrange, Act, and Assert phases for readability.
@BeforeEach runs before each test; @BeforeAll runs once per class -- use the right one for shared vs per-test fixtures.
Parameterized tests run the same logic with different inputs, reducing test code duplication.
assertThrows and assertAll are JUnit 5 lambda-based assertions that improve expressiveness over JUnit 4.
The extension model (@ExtendWith) replaces @RunWith and allows composable, multiple extensions per test class.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: JUnit is the standard unit-testing framework for Java. It provides annotations like @Test, @BeforeEach, and @AfterEach to mark test methods and lifecycle hooks, assertion methods like assertEquals and assertThrows to verify expected behavior, and a test runner that executes everything and reports pass or fail. It exists because manual testing does not scale and because without automated tests, refactoring becomes risky -- you are afraid to touch working code because you cannot verify it still works. A good unit test follows the AAA pattern: Arrange the preconditions, Act by calling the method, and Assert the outcome. I write each test to verify a single behavior, use parameterized tests to cover multiple inputs without duplication, and rely on Mockito to isolate the unit from its dependencies. In JUnit 5, I particularly like assertThrows for exception testing and the extension model for composable test setup.

question: Why is unit testing important in software development?
title: Why Unit Testing is Important | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Unit testing** means writing automated checks for one small piece of code — usually a single class or method — in isolation. It matters because it catches bugs early when they're cheap to fix, **prevents regressions** during refactoring, and acts as **executable documentation**. The business case is the cost curve: a bug caught in a unit test is roughly **10–100x cheaper** to fix than the same bug found in production.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying tests are 'a best practice' without quantifying the payoff, or assuming tests slow you down because you only count the upfront cost and ignore the debugging time saved
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Quote the exponential cost-of-fixing curve and frame tests as a refactoring safety net — the bigger the net, the bolder you can change code

sections.title: Why Unit Testing Matters
sections.content:
A **unit test** is an automated check for the smallest testable piece of code — one class or method — run in isolation from databases, networks, and other classes. Each test follows three steps: set up inputs, call the code, and verify the output matches what you expected.

The real value is **feedback speed** and **risk reduction**. Every line you write encodes an assumption about behavior; a unit test validates that assumption in milliseconds, at your desk, instead of days later in QA or production. Tests also serve as **living documentation** — a new developer reads `shouldApply10PercentDiscountForPremiumCustomers` and instantly knows the rule. The biggest payoff is **refactoring confidence**: with a green suite, you can restructure a module and know immediately if you broke anything.

amber|Living documentation|~Tests describe the rules|names read like specs|never goes stale like comments|onboard new devs faster

sections.title: A Unit Test for a Discount Service
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **"Tests slow me down."** They cost ~10-20% upfront but save far more by killing slow manual re-testing and production firefighting. Velocity goes up over time.
- **Testing only the happy path.** Real bugs hide in edge cases — null inputs, empty lists, negative amounts, boundaries. One success-case test is false confidence.
- **Writing tests you never run.** Tests that don't run in CI rot and start failing on unrelated changes. A test is only valuable if it runs automatically.
- **Asserting nothing.** Calling the method but skipping the assertion makes coverage rise while proving nothing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cost curve** — a bug caught in a unit test is 10-100x cheaper than the same bug in production.
- **Regression net** — re-running the suite after every change proves existing behavior still holds.
- **Living docs** — a well-named test documents the expected behavior better than a comment.
- **Refactor with confidence** — green tests mean a restructure preserved behavior.
- **Design signal** — code that is painful to test is usually too tightly coupled.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Unit testing means writing automated checks for one small piece of code at a time — usually a single class or method — in isolation from things like the database or the network. Each test sets up some inputs, calls the code, and verifies the output is what I expected.

The main reason it matters is the cost of fixing bugs. If I catch a logic error in a unit test, I fix it in a couple of minutes at my desk while the context is fresh. If that same bug reaches production, it might take hours to even reproduce, plus a hotfix deployment, and it could affect real users. Studies put that gap at ten to a hundred times more expensive. So unit tests compress the feedback loop from weeks down to seconds.

The second reason is regression safety. Say I refactor a payment method. If I have tests covering the scenarios, I just run them and instantly know whether I broke anything. Without tests, I'd have to manually re-test every flow or risk shipping a bug. That safety net is what lets me refactor boldly.

The third reason is documentation. A test named shouldApplyTenPercentDiscountForPremiumCustomers tells the next developer exactly how the rule works, and unlike a comment it can't go stale, because it has to pass.

A common fresher mistake is thinking tests slow you down. They cost a bit upfront, but you save far more by not debugging mysterious production issues. The other mistake is testing only the happy path — the real bugs live in the edge cases like null or negative values. To stand out, I'd mention that exponential cost curve as the business case for testing.

question: What is the difference between unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests?
title: Unit vs Integration vs E2E Tests | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Unit tests** verify a single class in isolation with dependencies mocked — fast and pinpoint-precise. **Integration tests** check several components together (e.g. a service hitting a real database) — slower but catch interface and SQL mismatches. **End-to-end tests** drive the full stack through the UI or API — slowest and most brittle. The **test pyramid** says: many unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, very few E2E tests on top.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the test pyramid and pick the cheapest test level that catches a given class of bug
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Inverting the pyramid — relying on slow, flaky E2E tests for logic that a fast unit test would cover, leading to 30-minute CI runs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the pyramid explicitly and explain why its shape balances speed, precision, and confidence

sections.title: The Test Pyramid
sections.content:
The **test pyramid** is a strategy for balancing test types by cost. At the **base** are **unit tests** — one class or method with all dependencies mocked. They run in milliseconds and pinpoint the exact line that failed. In the **middle** are **integration tests** — multiple real components wired together, like a repository hitting a real database. They're slower but catch bugs unit tests can't see: wrong SQL, JSON mapping errors, transaction issues. At the **top** are **end-to-end (E2E)** tests — a real user flow through UI and backend. They prove the whole system works but are slow and fragile.

The shape matters: thousands of unit tests, hundreds of integration tests, dozens of E2E tests. Inverting it — mostly E2E — gives slow CI and flaky failures.

sections.title: The Pyramid at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Unit (base)|~One class, mocked deps|runs in milliseconds|exact failure location|write the most of these
blue|Integration (middle)|~Real components together|seconds to run|catches SQL/JSON/contract bugs|write a moderate number
rose|End-to-end (top)|~Full stack, real user|minutes to run|brittle, breaks on UI change|keep to a critical few

sections.title: Unit vs Integration vs End-to-End
sections.content:
| Aspect | Unit Test | Integration Test | End-to-End Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | Single class/method | A few real components | Full workflow, UI to DB |
| **Dependencies** | All mocked/stubbed | Some real (DB, HTTP) | All real (browser, APIs, DB) |
| **Speed** | Milliseconds | Seconds | Minutes |
| **Failure precision** | Exact line | Interaction between parts | "Something broke somewhere" |
| **Maintenance** | Low, stable | Medium, schema changes | High, UI changes break it |
| **Tools** | JUnit 5 + Mockito | @SpringBootTest, Testcontainers | Selenium, RestAssured |

sections.title: Wrong instinct: drive logic through a slow E2E test
Right level: a fast unit test for the calculation
When to Use Each Level
sections.content: Use **unit tests** for business logic — discount math, validation, algorithms — anything that takes inputs and returns outputs. You want thousands. Use **integration tests** when crossing a boundary: a repository writing to PostgreSQL, a client calling a REST API. These catch a renamed column or a changed JSON field — contract bugs unit tests mock away. You want hundreds. Use **E2E tests** for the 5-10 most critical user journeys: login, checkout, payment. Don't push every edge case to E2E; when one fails, you still need unit tests to localize the bug.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pyramid shape** — many unit, fewer integration, very few E2E; this balances speed and confidence.
- **Unit** — single class, mocked deps, milliseconds, exact failure location.
- **Integration** — real DB/HTTP, seconds, catches contract/SQL mismatches.
- **E2E** — full stack, minutes, brittle; reserve for critical flows.
- **Inverted pyramid** — mostly E2E means slow, flaky CI nobody trusts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The difference really comes down to scope and speed. A unit test checks one class or method in complete isolation. Say I have an order service that calculates shipping. In a unit test I'd mock the database and any external calls, then test just the calculation. It runs in a few milliseconds, and if it fails I know exactly which line broke.

An integration test checks several real components working together. For that same service I'd spin up a real test database and verify it can save an order and read it back. That catches things a unit test can't see, like a wrong SQL query or a missing column. It's slower, maybe half a second, because something real is involved.

An end-to-end test simulates an actual user. I'd use something like Selenium to open a browser, log in, add items to the cart, and check out. That exercises the whole stack — UI, backend, database. It's the slowest, maybe thirty seconds, and when it fails I have to dig through logs to find where.

The key idea is the test pyramid. You want lots of unit tests because they're fast and stable, a moderate number of integration tests to catch cross-component bugs, and only a handful of end-to-end tests for critical flows like payment. A common fresher mistake is inverting that pyramid — leaning on end-to-end tests because they feel realistic — which gives you a slow, flaky suite nobody trusts. To stand out, I'd name the pyramid and explain why its shape balances speed, precision, and confidence.

question: What is TDD (Test-Driven Development) and what are its benefits?
title: TDD Test-Driven Development Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **TDD (Test-Driven Development)** is a cycle where you write a failing test first, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor while tests stay green — the **Red-Green-Refactor** loop. Writing the test first forces you to design the API from the caller's view, guarantees coverage by construction, and surfaces bad design early because hard-to-test code signals tight coupling.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Red-Green-Refactor as a design discipline, not just 'writing tests', and have actually practiced it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing TDD with writing tests after the code; writing too much in the Green phase; or skipping Refactor entirely
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that TDD is a design tool — if a class is painful to test in the Red step, that's early feedback to reduce coupling

sections.title: Test-Driven Development: Test First, Then Code
sections.content:
**Test-Driven Development (TDD)** flips the usual order: the test comes before the implementation. You work in tiny cycles called **Red-Green-Refactor**. **Red** — write a test for behavior that doesn't exist yet, so it fails; this forces you to decide the method's name, inputs, and outputs from the caller's perspective. **Green** — write the simplest code that makes the test pass, even a hardcoded value; the goal is a green bar, not elegance. **Refactor** — clean up duplication and names while the tests stay green, using them as a safety net.

The deeper benefit is **design feedback**: if a class is hard to test, it usually has too many dependencies or does too much — TDD makes you feel that pain before you've sunk hours into it.

sections.title: The Red-Green-Refactor Loop
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["RED
Write a failing test
for new behavior"] --> B["GREEN
Write the simplest
code to pass"] B --> C["REFACTOR
Clean up while
tests stay green"] C --> A C --> D["Feature done?
Move to next test"] ```

sections.title: Worked Example: Building a Password Validator
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling test-after "TDD."** TDD specifically means the test comes first; tests written afterward tend to describe what the code does, not what it should do.
- **Over-building in Green.** Writing the whole feature once the test compiles. Write only enough to pass; add complexity in the next cycle.
- **Skipping Refactor.** Green tests don't mean clean code. Refactoring while green is when you pay down duplication safely.
- **Testing implementation, not behavior.** Verifying private calls makes tests break on every refactor even when behavior is unchanged.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Red-Green-Refactor** — failing test, minimal code to pass, clean up while green; repeat in minutes.
- **Test-first designs the API** — you decide name, inputs, outputs from the caller's side first.
- **Coverage by construction** — every line exists because a test demanded it.
- **Design feedback** — needing five mocks to test a class is a coupling smell TDD exposes early.
- **Green phase rule** — simplest code that passes, even a hardcoded return.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
TDD stands for Test-Driven Development, and it's a cycle where you write the test before the code. The loop has three steps: Red, Green, Refactor. Red means I write a test for a feature that doesn't exist yet, so it fails. That forces me to think about what the method should do — its name, its inputs, its outputs — before I write any implementation. Green means I write the simplest possible code to make that test pass. I'm not trying to build the perfect solution, just enough to turn the bar green; sometimes that's even a hardcoded value, and that's fine. Refactor means I clean up the code while keeping the tests green — remove duplication, improve names, extract methods — and the tests are my safety net proving I didn't change behavior.

The big benefit is that TDD drives better design. If a class is hard to test, it's usually because it has too many dependencies or it's doing too much. TDD makes me feel that pain upfront. For example, if I'm writing a test for an order service and I realize I need to mock five things, that's a design smell telling me to rethink the responsibilities. TDD also guarantees coverage, because every line of code exists to satisfy a test.

A common mistake is confusing TDD with just writing tests — TDD specifically means test first; writing tests afterward doesn't give you the design benefit. Another is writing too much code in the green phase. To stand out, I'd say TDD is really a design tool, not just a testing technique — the tests give you feedback on coupling before you've invested hours.

question: What makes a good unit test?
title: Good Unit Test Characteristics | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: A good unit test follows **FIRST**: **Fast** (milliseconds), **Independent** (no shared state, any order), **Repeatable** (same result everywhere — no reliance on time or randomness), **Self-validating** (clear pass/fail, no log reading), and **Timely** (written close to the code). It also tests **one behavior**, has a **descriptive name**, and follows **Arrange-Act-Assert**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you've written real tests and learned what makes them maintainable vs brittle and flaky
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Tests that depend on execution order, share mutable static state, or assert several unrelated behaviors in one method
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name FIRST and give a concrete bad-test fix — e.g. removing shared static state that caused random CI failures

sections.title: What Makes a Unit Test Good
sections.content:
Good unit tests follow the **FIRST** principles. **Fast** — they run in milliseconds so developers run them constantly; slow tests get skipped. **Independent** — each test runs alone or in any order with no shared state. **Repeatable** — same result on any machine at any time; no dependence on the current time or random data. **Self-validating** — a clear pass or fail with no manual log inspection. **Timely** — written close to the production code, ideally before it.

Beyond FIRST, a good test has a **descriptive name** that reads like a spec, tests **one behavior** so a failure points to one cause, and follows **Arrange-Act-Assert** for structure.

sections.title: FIRST at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Fast|~Runs in milliseconds|no DB, network, or file I/O|mock slow dependencies|so devs run it constantly
blue|Independent|~Any order, runs alone|no shared static state|sets up its own data|enables parallel execution
amber|Repeatable|~Same result everywhere|no System.currentTimeMillis|inject a Clock|no flaky failures
violet|Self-validating|~Clear pass or fail|real assertions, not prints|no manual log reading|CI can gate on it
cyan|Timely|~Written close to code|ideally test-first|edge cases still fresh|coverage stays high

sections.title: A Bad Test: shared state, vague name, multiple behaviors
Good Tests: independent, named, one behavior each
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Order-dependent tests.** Static fields or a shared DB that accumulates state; test 3 passes only if test 1 ran first. Breaks parallel runs.
- **Multiple behaviors per test.** Checking discount, inventory, and email in one method; a failure doesn't tell you which broke.
- **Vague names.** `testService` or `testCase1` say nothing; prefer `shouldRejectOrderWhenInventoryInsufficient`.
- **Brittle assertions.** Asserting exact string formatting or internal calls makes refactors break tests even when behavior is unchanged.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **FIRST** — Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely.
- **One behavior per test** — it should fail for exactly one reason.
- **Descriptive names** — `shouldApplyDiscountForPremiumMembers` reads like a spec.
- **Arrange-Act-Assert** — set up, call, verify, in three clear steps.
- **No shared state** — each test builds its own data; never rely on order.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A good unit test follows the FIRST principles. FIRST stands for Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, and Timely. Fast means it runs in milliseconds — if you have a thousand tests and each takes a second, nobody runs them, so you keep them fast by mocking slow things like databases and HTTP calls. Independent means each test can run alone or in any order; it sets up its own data and doesn't rely on state left behind by another test. Repeatable means it gives the same result every time — no flaky failures because it depends on the current time or a random number. Self-validating means it clearly passes or fails without me reading logs to interpret the result. And Timely means I write it close to the code, ideally before it if I'm doing TDD.

Beyond FIRST, a good test has a name that explains the scenario. Instead of testOrder, I'd name it shouldApplyTenPercentDiscountForPremiumCustomers, so it reads like a specification. It should also test one behavior, because if a single test checks discount and inventory and a failure happens, I can't tell which part broke.

A common fresher mistake is writing tests that depend on each other through a shared static field, so test three only passes if test one ran first — that breaks the moment tests run in parallel. Another is asserting on implementation details, which makes tests fail on every refactor. To stand out, I'd mention a concrete fix, like removing shared static state that was causing random failures in CI and making each test build its own data.

seo.metaTitle: Good Unit Test Characteristics Java | Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn what makes a good unit test for Java fresher interviews. FIRST principles, AAA pattern, test behavior not implementation explained.

speakable_v2.standard_example: JUnit 5 tests for a Spring Boot service class with @Test and assertions
speakable_v2.hook: A slow, flaky, or shared-state test is almost worse than no test — it erodes trust. The FIRST acronym gives you the checklist to avoid that.

beats.text: FIRST stands for Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, and Timely. It's a checklist of five properties that make a unit test reliable, trustworthy, and maintainable.
Tests that violate FIRST properties fail intermittently, run slowly, or get abandoned. The acronym helps teams catch these issues during code review before bad habits compound.

items: Fast: runs in milliseconds — no database, no network, no file I/O
Independent: each test sets up its own state; running in any order gives the same result
Repeatable: same result on any machine at any time — no dependency on current time or randomness
Self-validating: test clearly passes or fails — no manual log inspection
Timely: written close to the code, ideally before it in TDD

beats.text: A test that calls System.currentTimeMillis() directly is not Repeatable — it'll behave differently depending on when it runs. The fix is to inject a Clock and use Clock.fixed() in tests. sharp edge: a test that passes alone but fails in a suite usually violates Independent — it's sharing mutable state with another test without realizing it.

items: Tests that rely on execution order — classic sign of shared state, violates Independent
Missing assertions in a test body — the test 'passes' because it never checks anything, violates Self-validating

speakable_v2.cap: Violate any FIRST property and your tests become unreliable — developers stop trusting them and stop running them.

question: What is code coverage and what is a good coverage target?
title: Code Coverage Java Testing | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Code coverage** measures the percentage of code executed while tests run — common types are **line**, **branch**, and **method** coverage (JaCoCo is the standard Java tool). A healthy target for business logic is **70-80%**, but coverage is **necessary, not sufficient**: you can hit 100% with tests that execute code yet assert nothing. Treat it as a floor that finds untested code, not a goal.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you see coverage as a gap-finding metric, not the goal — and know branch coverage is stricter than line coverage
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing 100% coverage means good tests, which leads to trivial assert-nothing tests that game the number
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that 100% line coverage can still miss branches, and that a test with no assertions raises coverage but proves nothing

sections.title: Understanding Code Coverage
sections.content:
**Code coverage** measures what percentage of your code executes when the test suite runs. **Line coverage** tracks which lines ran, **branch coverage** tracks which if/else paths were taken, and **method coverage** tracks which methods were called. Tools like **JaCoCo** generate HTML reports highlighting covered lines in green and uncovered in red.

The key insight: coverage is **necessary but not sufficient**. You can reach 100% with tests that call every method but assert nothing — the lines ran, the number went up, but nothing was verified. Treat coverage as a **floor**, not a ceiling: use it to find untested code, especially high-risk areas like payments, and aim for quality assertions rather than chasing 100%.

sections.title: Coverage Types & Targets
sections.content:
emerald|Line coverage|~Which lines executed|simplest metric|easy to inflate|baseline only
blue|Branch coverage|~Which if/else paths ran|stricter than line|catches untested else|target 70-80% on logic
violet|Method coverage|~Which methods called|coarse-grained|misses internal branches|use as a quick scan
amber|The trap|~Coverage != quality|100% with no asserts|proves nothing|measure what tests verify

sections.title: Line Coverage vs Branch Coverage
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Chasing 100%.** It pushes people to write assert-nothing tests that inflate the number without catching bugs.
- **Ignoring branch coverage.** 100% line coverage can hide untested `else` paths — branch coverage is the stricter signal.
- **Testing trivial code.** Covering getters, setters, and generated `equals`/`hashCode` raises the number with zero value.
- **Not checking what's uncovered.** 65% overall is fine — unless the missing 35% is payment validation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Types** — line (lines run), branch (if/else paths), method (methods called).
- **Targets** — 70-80% on business logic; skip trivial getters/DTOs.
- **Necessary, not sufficient** — 100% with no assertions proves nothing.
- **Branch > line** — full line coverage can still miss else branches.
- **JaCoCo** — standard Java tool; `mvn test jacoco:report` builds the HTML report.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Code coverage measures the percentage of your code that runs when the tests execute. There are a few types. Line coverage tracks which lines ran. Branch coverage tracks which if-else paths you took. Method coverage tracks which methods were called. A tool like JaCoCo generates a report showing this, usually green for covered and red for uncovered.

A good target depends on the code. For business logic like payment processing or discount rules, I'd aim for seventy to eighty percent. For trivial code like getters and auto-generated methods, I wouldn't chase coverage at all. The key point I'd make is that high coverage is necessary but not sufficient. You can hit a hundred percent with tests that don't actually verify anything — for example, a test that calls every method but never asserts on the result. The lines ran, so coverage goes up, but the test proves nothing. So I treat coverage as a floor, not a goal. If critical code sits at forty percent, that's a problem and I write more tests; but I don't pad the number with meaningless tests.

One mistake freshers make is assuming a hundred percent coverage means the tests are good — it doesn't; you have to look at what the tests actually check. Another is ignoring branch coverage. A method can have full line coverage but only fifty percent branch coverage if you never tested the else paths. To stand out, I'd say coverage is really a tool to find gaps — and in code review, if someone adds two hundred lines of logic and coverage doesn't move, that's a red flag.

items: Line/statement coverage: simplest — what percentage of lines ran?
